title: A Snake Expert Was Bitten and Took Notes on His Own Death, Hour by Hour

scenes.text: A snake bit this scientist. He took notes.
Chicago, September 1957. Karl Schmidt of the Field Museum picks up a young boomslang sent over from the zoo. It bites his left thumb.
He believes a snake that small can't deliver a fatal dose. No boomslang antivenom exists in America anyway. So he takes the train home.
His diary: 4:30, strong nausea. 5:30, chills and a fever of 101.7. Then his gums begin to bleed.
Boomslang venom stops blood from clotting. By morning he is bleeding internally, and just before 3 PM he is dead, about 24 hours after the bite.
His notebook is still at the museum. The last science he ever did was on himself.

description:
In September 1957, herpetologist Karl Patterson Schmidt was bitten by a young boomslang at Chicago's Field Museum, assumed the dose could not be fatal, and recorded his symptoms hour by hour in his diary as he went home.
Boomslang venom stops the blood from clotting; he died of internal bleeding about 24 hours after the bite.
Would you have gone to the hospital, or kept writing?
subject: boomslang snake
first_comment: Only one fang went in, about 3 millimetres deep. A 2017 study found boomslang venom is over 75 percent clot-destroying enzymes. Which snake should we cover next?
